2009: A nation divided

Ten months ago, on the afternoon of February 16th, bombs tore through the West Wing of the White House and the House chamber of the Capitol, killing the President, the Vice President, the Speaker of the House and the President pro tempore of the Senate. Attorney General Raymond E. Calloway, the designated survivor, took the oath of office that night at an undisclosed location. What followed has no precedent in American history. The federal government moved to Sacramento in March. Within weeks, a self-proclaimed Republic of Gilead had seized much of New England, several states and regions declared themselves independent or "armed neutral", Alaska and South Texas were placed under military administration, and across most of the country the news simply stopped - no broadcasts, no wire reports, no phone service. Since August, five nuclear devices have been detonated on American soil, the latest on November 4th near Millington, Tennessee. Photographers have worked under curfews, at checkpoints and, in some places, at real risk to their lives; several of the images below were carried out of closed areas by hand. The Big Picture, like the rest of Boston.com, is now produced by Globe staff working outside of Boston. Collected here are 24 photographs from a year that is not yet over. (24 photos total)

California Army National Guard soldiers stand behind concertina wire on Capitol Mall in Sacramento, California on the morning of November 5, 2009, the day after a nuclear device was detonated near Millington, Tennessee. The California State Capitol, background, has housed the executive branch of the federal government since March. (REUTERS/Mark Halvorsen)

2
Members of the Interim Congress meet in the Sacramento Memorial Auditorium on May 28, 2009, during the body's first week in session. The Interim Congress, formed by surviving members from western states and senators appointed under state law, has met at the 1927 auditorium since the Capitol building in Washington was declared unsafe. (AP Photo/Dana Whitcomb) #

3
Customers and staff at a diner on J Street in Sacramento watch acting President Raymond E. Calloway address the nation on the evening of November 4, 2009. In his eight-minute statement, Calloway said the government "will find those responsible, wherever they are hiding," and asked the Interim Congress for emergency powers. (Gene Lattimore/The Sacramento Bee) #

4
Rows of FEMA tents fill a parking lot at Cal Expo, the California state fairgrounds in Sacramento, on September 19, 2009. Nearly 31,000 people evacuated from Contra Costa and Solano counties after the August 9th detonations in Concord and at Mare Island were still living at the site in late November, according to state officials. (Justin Okafor/Getty Images) #

5
A fence marks the edge of the exclusion zone on a residential street in Vallejo, California, about 2.5 miles from the former Mare Island Naval Shipyard, on October 3, 2009. Residents of roughly 9,000 homes inside the fence have been allowed back only once, for two hours, to collect belongings. (REUTERS/Mark Halvorsen) #

6
Armed volunteers watch a farmer drive past a roadblock on a levee road in Sutter County, California on November 12, 2009. The road runs close to the Butte-Sutter line, the boundary agreed under the June Red Bluff Accord between the federal government and the State of Jefferson. The Sutter Buttes are visible in the distance. (Gene Lattimore/The Sacramento Bee) #

7
Cars abandoned by fleeing drivers remain on Interstate 40 east of Kingman, Arizona on August 27, 2009, seventeen days after a nuclear device was detonated near Kingman Airport. The photograph was made by a photographer who drove in from Las Vegas along the federal Interstate 15 corridor. (AP Photo/Robert Castellano) #

8
Airmen unload pallets of bottled water and food from a C-130 at Biggs Army Airfield in El Paso, Texas on October 21, 2009. With roads into the city cut off on three sides, El Paso has been supplied almost entirely by air since June. (Lucas Brenner/AFP/Getty Images) #

9
U.S. Army soldiers keep watch from a sandbagged position on the southern perimeter of Fort Bliss in El Paso, Texas, on November 9, 2009. Mexican Army units have occupied positions across much of southern New Mexico and west Texas since July, in what Mexico City describes as a temporary "humanitarian security zone". (Lucas Brenner/AFP/Getty Images) #

10
Sailors and civilian volunteers unload relief supplies from a Navy supply ship in Corpus Christi, Texas on October 14, 2009. The South Texas Protectorate, administered by the military from Naval Air Station Corpus Christi and Kingsville since May, is home to an estimated 1.4 million people. (AP Photo/Alma Reyes) #

11
Residents of the Frayser neighborhood of north Memphis, Tennessee, watch the glow of fires on the northern horizon on the evening of November 4, 2009, about five hours after a nuclear device estimated at 10 to 15 kilotons was detonated near Naval Support Activity Mid-South in Millington. Memphis lies inside the silent zone; this and the following three photographs were carried out by road and transmitted from Dallas on November 9. (Terrence Booker for The Associated Press) #

12
Traffic crawls south on Interstate 55 toward Mississippi as residents leave Memphis on November 5, 2009. Authorities ordered people within 30 miles of Millington to shelter in place, but tens of thousands left by car anyway; the 40-mile drive to Hernando took some drivers more than nine hours. (AP Photo/Kyle Danner) #

13
A National Guard soldier checks a girl for radioactive contamination at a screening station in Hernando, Mississippi on November 5, 2009. Guard officers at the station said fewer than one in 200 people screened there needed decontamination. (REUTERS/Paul Whitaker) #

14
Evacuees from the Memphis area rest on cots in a high school gymnasium in Olive Branch, Mississippi on November 7, 2009. Volunteers said the school was sheltering more than 600 people, most of whom had left north Memphis on foot or by car on the night of the blast. (Terrence Booker for The Associated Press) #

15
Members of a county volunteer company stand outside the Washington County Courthouse in Jonesborough, Franklin on November 6, 2009. Franklin, which declared "armed neutrality" in March, has called up volunteers to guard its borders with Tennessee and Virginia. Governor Harlan D. Ketron said there was "no indication of any fallout risk" to the state after the Millington blast. (Ray Sizemore/Johnson City Press) #

16
The skyline of Kansas City, Missouri is dark in this photograph made from an overpass on Interstate 70 on October 24, 2009. Kansas City is one of hundreds of cities inside the so-called "silent zone", where broadcast, telephone and Internet service ended in the spring. The photograph was carried out by a freelance photographer and transmitted from Denver. (Name withheld for safety/AP) #

17
A family eats Thanksgiving dinner by candlelight at their farmhouse in Holmes County, Ohio on November 26, 2009. The family said they have not had electric power since April, and get news from a battery radio that picks up a Canadian station at night. The photograph was carried across the Pennsylvania line and made available to news organizations on Saturday. (Name withheld for safety/REUTERS) #

18
State of Lincoln volunteers check vehicles on a bridge over the Spokane River in Spokane, Washington on March 2, 2009, ten days after Lincoln declared independence from Washington state. Checkpoints on bridges into downtown Spokane were removed in June, then reinstated after the Millington blast. (Sara Lindqvist/The Spokesman-Review) #

19
People wait for bread and canned food outside a downtown church in Spokane on November 14, 2009. Food banks in the State of Lincoln say demand has tripled since rail traffic from the Puget Sound region was halted in the summer. (Sara Lindqvist/The Spokesman-Review) #

20
Residents wait with gas cans at a station in Marquette, in the State of Superior, on November 18, 2009, as a deputy keeps order. Fuel in Michigan's former Upper Peninsula has been rationed to five gallons per household per week since the Mackinac Bridge was closed. (Erik Halonen/The Mining Journal) #

21
Police cruisers and concrete barriers block the northern approach to the Mackinac Bridge at St. Ignace on March 28, 2009, the morning after Superior's declaration of statehood. The five-mile bridge has been closed to all but authorized freight since. (AP Photo/Carl Jorgensen) #

22
A military convoy travels the Glenn Highway near Anchorage, Alaska on November 3, 2009. Alaska has been under military administration from Elmendorf Air Force Base and Fort Richardson since March; civilian travel between communities requires a permit. (Ben Tolliver/Anchorage Daily News) #

23
A guard stands at a new barrier on the Harvard Bridge between Cambridge and Boston, Massachusetts, in this undated photograph believed to have been made in October 2009. Gilead authorities closed all but two crossings of the Charles River in the spring. The photograph was smuggled out of the region and obtained by Reuters. (REUTERS/Stringer) #

24
Two women in red robes and white bonnets walk past shuttered shops in downtown Boston in this undated photograph believed to have been made in November 2009. Residents who have left the region describe new rules requiring some women to wear prescribed clothing in public. Boston.com could not independently verify the circumstances in which the photograph was taken. (REUTERS/Stringer) #
